questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
- Tests ability to wire ConfigMaps and Secrets across a namespace, plus InitContainer usage and lifecycle hooks.
- Evaluates observability via a metrics endpoint and logs on a PVC, with a simple autoscale path via HPA.
- Probes, resource requests, and minimal skeletons show readiness for real-world CKAD constraints.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap/Secret integration, InitContainer tooling, PVC-backed logs, custom metrics exposure, readiness/liveness, HPA kinship, minimal YAML.

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: feature-tester
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: feature-tester
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: feature-tester
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: init-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache httpie jq && mkdir -p /logs"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: tester
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do for url in $(cat /etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints); do resp=$(http --ignore-stdin GET "$url" Authorization:"Bearer $(cat /secret/api_token)"); echo "$url -> $resp" >> /logs/$(date +%s).log; done; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: ENDPOINTS_CONFIG
          value: "/etc/feature-endpoints/endpoints"
        - name: TOKEN_SECRET
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: api-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          name: metrics
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "256Mi"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: feature-tester-logs
      - name: feature-endpoints
        configMap:
          name: feature-endpoints
      - name: secret
        secret:
          secretName: api-token
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
  
# Note: This is a minimal skeleton; real manifests should separate concerns (InitContainer, metrics, status storage) and handle errors gracefully.
```

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: per-namespace scope, Pod image inspection, external API interaction, and secure data handling with Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVCs.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped Deployments and Pods
- InitContainers for bootstrap tasks
- Secrets for API tokens and minimal exposure
- ConfigMaps for status storage
- PVC-based log streaming
- NetworkPolicy to restrict egress
- Probes for reliability and readiness

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ns-security-baseline
  namespace: <target-namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh","-c","apk add --no-cache curl jq || true"]
      containers:
      - name: baseline-scanner
        image: registry.example/scanner:latest
        env:
        - name: CVE_API_URL
          value: "https://cve-feed.example/api/v1/cves"
        - name: API_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: cve-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ns-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you rotate the Secret token without downtime?
- How would you scale the scanner across namespaces while keeping per-namespace isolation?

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace operational hardening: config-driven behavior, rolling restarts, health checks, lifecycle hooks, and disruption budgets in CKAD context.

Key Concepts
- ConfigMap-driven behavior with pod template checksum for rolling restarts
- Tail/log ingestion from a PVC-backed path
- Probes: readiness /healthz, liveness /livez
- Resource requests/limits and lifecycle preStop
- PodDisruptionBudget to guarantee minimum healthy pods

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: log-processor
  namespace: audit
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<checksum-from-configmap>"
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: myrepo/log-processor:latest
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /var/log/stream
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 10"]
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: log-stream-pvc
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate rolling restarts trigger on ConfigMap updates?
- How would you simulate load and verify throughput vs. reliability?
- How would you rollback to a previous ConfigMap or image version?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical security hardening and runtime verification in CKAD scope, including namespace policies, container security, probes, and network controls.

## Key Concepts
- PodSecurity via namespace labels
- SecurityContext: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, capabilities
- Probes: readiness and liveness
- PreStop lifecycle
- ConfigMap mounting and rolling restarts via checksum
- NetworkPolicy egress control

## Code Example
```yaml
# Minimal patch sketch (Deployment + NetworkPolicy)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: logger
  namespace: logging
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: logger
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: logger
        image: registry.example/logger:1.0
        securityContext:
          runAsNonRoot: true
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          capabilities:
            drop: ["ALL"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: cfg
          mountPath: /etc/logger
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /livez
            port: 8080
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep 5"]
      volumes:
      - name: cfg
        configMap:
          name: logger-config
```

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: logger-egress
  namespace: logging
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: logger
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 9200
```

- How would you test the rollback path if the ConfigMap causes a regression?
- How would you audit namespace security changes for compliance?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests orchestration across namespaces, dynamic Job creation per image, and the use of InitContainers, PVCs, and ConfigMaps to surface results. It also evaluates network isolation and RBAC scoping in real CKAD-like constraints.

## Key Concepts

- CronJob driving cross-namespace work
- Ephemeral per-image Jobs
- InitContainer installation of scanners (e.g., Trivy)
- Persistent Logs via PVC (/logs)
- Per-image status in a ConfigMap (scan-status)
- Namespace NetworkPolicy restricting egress to vuln DB/scanner API
- Readiness/Liveness probes and cleanup/idempotency

## Code Example

```yaml
# Minimal skeleton: CronJob in audit namespace
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: image-scan-cron
  namespace: audit
spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          serviceAccountName: audit-scan-sa
          volumes:
            - name: logs
              persistentVolumeClaim:
                claimName: image-scan-logs
          containers:
            - name: scanner
              image: registry.example/scanner:latest
              command: ["bash","-c","/usr/local/bin/scan.sh"]
              volumeMounts:
                - name: logs
                  mountPath: /logs
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you scale this when a namespace has thousands of Pods/images?  
- How would you handle scan result retention and cleanup of completed Jobs?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: mounting PVCs, ConfigMaps as files/env, InitContainers to install utilities, Secrets, TLS sidecar, probes, and a Namespace NetworkPolicy. It enforces a clean, minimal design with explicit security and ops considerations.

## Key Concepts
- PVCs and ConfigMaps usage in Pods
- InitContainer lifecycle and isolated image
- Secret handling and basic-auth setup
- TLS cert rotation via a sidecar pattern
- Readiness/Liveness probes and namespace NetworkPolicy scope

## Code Example
```yaml
# skeleton Deployment/Pod with InitContainer, main nginx container, and volumes
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-frontend
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-frontend
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-frontend
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:stable-alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        volumeMounts:
        - name: www
          mountPath: /www
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      - name: tls-sidecar
        image: alpine:edge
        args: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "sleep infinity"]
        # placeholder for cert-rotation mechanism
      initContainers:
      - name: install-nginx
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-cache nginx curl jq && mkdir -p /www && echo done"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: www
          mountPath: /www
      volumes:
      - name: www
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: web-www-pvc
      imagePullSecrets:
      - name: regcred
      nodeSelector: {}
      tolerations: []
      affinity: {}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this for multiple namespaces with a shared ingress?
- What are the trade-offs of placing config in ConfigMap vs environment variables for this app?

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1

metadata:
```

## Why This Is Asked

This question tests hands-on CKAD skills: in-cluster configuration, API access, and multi-resource coordination. It evaluates how the candidate wires ConfigMaps, Secrets, and PVCs into a Deployment, and how they enforce traffic restrictions with a NetworkPolicy.

## Key Concepts

- Namespace-scoped Deployment and RBAC permissions
- ConfigMap-based thresholds and Secret-based credentials
- API access to Namespace ResourceQuota metrics
- InitContainer usage for tools like curl/jq
- Logs persisted to a PVC mounted at /logs
- Readiness and liveness probes
- Namespace NetworkPolicy to restrict egress to the central endpoint

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: alert-config
data:
  cpu-threshold: "80"
  memory-threshold: "85"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: alert-credentials
data:
  api-key: <base64-encoded-key>
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: log-storage
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: resource-watcher
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: resource-watcher
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: installer
          image: busybox
          command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - |-
                wget -q https://github.com/stedolan/jq/releases/download/jq-1.6/jq-linux64 -O /usr/local/bin/jq
                chmod +x /usr/local/bin/jq
                apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tools
              mountPath: /usr/local/bin
      containers:
        - name: watcher
          image: your-watcher-image:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
              name: http
          env:
            - name: CENTRAL_ENDPOINT
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: alert-credentials
                  key: api-key
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /logs
            - name: config
              mountPath: /config
              readOnly: true
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "64Mi"
              cpu: "50m"
            limits:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: log-storage
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: alert-config
        - name: tools
          emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-restriction
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: resource-watcher
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              name: central-monitoring
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443
```

## Trade-offs

1. **Polling vs. Watch API**: Polling ResourceQuota is simpler but adds latency; the Watch API is more efficient but requires handling event streams.
2. **Sidecar vs. Main Container**: A sidecar could handle logging while the main container focuses on monitoring—improving separation of concerns.
3. **Centralized vs. Per-Namespace**: Deploying per-namespace increases resource usage but provides isolation and reduces blast radius.
4. **PVC for Logs**: Using a PVC adds persistence but requires storage provisioning; consider sidecar streaming to stdout for easier management.
5. **InitContainer Overhead**: Downloading tools on every pod start slows startup; a custom image with tools pre-installed would be faster.

## Key Concepts

```yaml
        spec:

            image: busybox

          containers:

            command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
            args:
            - |
              # Read policy from ConfigMap
              # Get all Deployments in namespace
              # Compare images against policy
              # Patch mismatched Deployments
              # Write heartbeat log to /logs
              # POST summary to policy-portal
            volumeMounts:
            - name: log-volume
              mountPath: /logs
            readinessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/ready"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 5
              periodSeconds: 10
            livenessProbe:
              exec:
                command: ["test", "-f", "/logs/alive"]
              initialDelaySeconds: 15

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

metadata:
  name: restrict-egress

  podSelector: {}

  - to:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: policy-portal
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Frequency**: Running every 5 minutes balances responsiveness vs. resource usage; longer intervals reduce API load but delay remediation
- **PVC vs. Sidecar**: Using a PVC is simpler but requires storage provisioning; a sidecar could stream logs directly
- **Patch vs. Reconcile Controller**: A declarative controller would be more robust but requires custom operator development; CronJob is quicker to implement but imperative
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installing tools increases pod startup time; consider using a custom image with tools baked in instead
- **NetworkPolicy**: Restricting egress improves security but may break legitimate communication; ensure all required endpoints are explicitly allowed

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to design Kubernetes-native backup patterns using CRD + Job orchestration, with proper use of InitContainers, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and PVs. Encourages thinking about per-namespace scoping, fault-tolerance, and minimal operator logic.

## Key Concepts
- CustomResourceDefinition and a namespace-scoped controller
- Jobs, InitContainers, and data packaging (tarball) for backups
- Secrets for credentials and ConfigMaps for configuration
- PVC usage for temporary/log data and readiness/liveness probes
- Idempotency, retries, and failure semantics

## Trade-offs Discussion

**Advantages:**
- Namespace isolation prevents cross-namespace interference
- Job-based approach provides built-in retry and failure handling
- InitContainers ensure dependencies are met before main workload
- Readiness/liveness probes provide operational visibility
- Secret/ConfigMap separation follows security best practices

**Limitations:**
- Requires custom controller for CRD watching and Job creation
- No incremental backup support (full tarball each time)
- AWS credentials stored in cluster (consider IRSA/EKS)
- No backup verification or restore automation
- PVC mounting requires proper permissions and access

**Alternatives:**
- Use Velero for comprehensive backup/restore solution
- Implement CSI snapshot for instant PVC backups
- Consider sidecar pattern for continuous backup
- Use CronJob instead of one-time Jobs for scheduled backups

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: image-scan

spec:
  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:
      app: image-scan
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: image-scan
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
```
